title: What do you prefer – human error or machine error?
author: Daisy Christodoulou
summary: Christodoulou weighs the trade-offs between human and machine error in assessing student writing, responding to pushback on AI marking. She credits machines with speed and scalability, noting that human quality falls as speed and volume rise, which makes comparison with average machine performance the fair one. Their weakness is that they do not decide as humans do, which she illustrates with the fennel-and-insurance correlation and older essay markers biased towards length. Deep learning models carry related risks of gaming and degradation, as pixel-level attacks on facial recognition show. Her answer is continual validation of the model by expert human judgement, and she proposes a 10 percent human and 90 percent AI split, though the post closes with a pitch for No More Marking's projects.
points: Human decision quality drops with speed and scale while machine quality scales, so the fair comparison is with average rather than exceptional human performance.
Machines decide differently from humans, so a correlate like length or fennel purchases can be rewarded and then gamed.
Opaque deep learning models can be fooled by tiny changes that no human assessor would notice, risking degradation over time.
Validation against expert human judgement must be continual, not a one-off, to guard an AI marker against gaming.
The recommended hybrid has humans judge 10 percent and AI 90 percent, saving time while every script is still seen twice by humans.
quotes: The great advantage that machines have over humans is their speed and scalability. They don’t get tired or fatigued or need breaks, and once you’ve trained one machine, it’s easy to train lots more.

The quality of human decision making gets worse if you increase the speed and scale. If you ask an individual human to make more decisions or to make them quicker, they will get start making mistakes.

A funny example from finance involves fennel purchases. A big insurance company cross-referenced their data with a supermarket loyalty scheme and found that purchases of fresh fennel were correlated with lower home insurance claims. Now you can speculate as to why this is, but it’s unlikely that purchasing fresh fennel causes people to claim less on insurance.

The corresponding issue with older AI marking models is that they are very biased towards length. Again, we can see why this is: length does correlate with quality in the same way buying fennel correlates with low insurance claims. But it doesn’t cause quality, and once people know that length is what is being rewarded, they have an incentive to write reams of gobbledegook.

For example, researchers have managed to successfully fool facial recognition technologies by changing just one or two pixels in an image. These changes would make no difference at all to a human assessor, but can cause the AI to change its mind about what’s in the image.

The solution to all these problems is validation. You need some way of using expert human judgement to validate your machine model. And this can’t be a one-off process: you have to continually validate your model to guard it against gaming.

This is why, in fields that are being overwhelmed with decisions, technology is so appealing. And this is why it isn’t fair to compare exceptional or even average human performance with average machine performance. You can easily scale up average machine performance. You can’t easily scale up average human performance (let alone exceptional human performance).
